title: Racing heart in a 24-year-old teacher
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 24-year-old woman in the ED with 30 minutes of sudden, fast, regular palpitations. The candidate then interprets her observations, 12-lead ECG and blood results (including thyroid function), recognises a supraventricular tachycardia with untreated hyperthyroidism (probable Graves' disease), and outlines management and safety netting.
focus: Palpitations: a focused history across systems, recognising SVT on the ECG, managing stable SVT and finding the thyrotoxic trigger
stem: You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Sarah, a 24-year-old woman, has come in saying she feels like her heart is racing. She is on a trolley in the acute area with a cardiac monitor attached. The triage nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sarah and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Act on anything the nurse tells you (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Sarah's observations, her 12-lead ECG and her blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sarah, a 24-year-old primary school teacher. You are sitting up on the trolley, anxious, with a hand on your chest. You can talk in full sentences but you are a little short of breath. A nurse is with the candidate and does what they ask. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

Opening line: "Doctor, my heart won't stop racing!"

History (give only when asked)

The palpitations

  • Started suddenly about 30 minutes ago (about 09:35) while you were sitting down. It came on "like a switch". It has not stopped since.
  • You have never had this before.
  • If asked to describe it, say: "It's just pounding, really fast."
  • If asked specifically whether it is regular or irregular, or asked to tap it out, say: "It's just consistently fast, I think it's a regular pattern," and tap a fast, regular rhythm on the table.
  • Nothing makes it worse. You tried slow breathing and relaxing and it has not helped.
  • You had to leave work to come in.

Other symptoms

  • Yes: mild shortness of breath that started shortly after the racing began. You feel slightly faint and dizzy. You feel more anxious and on edge, with no particular cause.
  • No: chest pain, fainting or blacking out, ankle swelling.

Other systems (give only if asked)

  • Thyroid: you have lost about 2 kg over the last 4 months without trying. You have felt warm even though the weather has been cold. Your bowel motions have been looser than usual. You have felt more anxious lately. No change in your periods.
  • Episodes and sweating: no previous episodes of palpitations, no attacks of sweating, no headaches with this.
  • Blood: nobody has said you look pale. You have been a little more tired than usual lately. No heavy periods and no bleeding from anywhere.
  • General: no fever, night sweats, rigors or chills.

Past medical history

  • Nil. No heart or thyroid problems. No asthma. No previous operations or hospital stays.
  • Immunisations up to date. No recent travel.

Medications and allergies

  • The oral contraceptive pill. You take it every day and do not think you could be pregnant.
  • No other prescription medicines. Nothing over the counter (no cold and flu tablets, no diet pills, no supplements).
  • No recreational drugs, ever.
  • No allergies.

Family history

  • Mother: coeliac disease. Father: well.
  • If asked: nobody in the family has died suddenly or young, and you do not know of anyone with a heart rhythm or thyroid problem.

Social history

  • Primary school teacher. You live alone.
  • Coffee: three cups a day.
  • Alcohol: 4 to 5 standard drinks a day on weekends.
  • Non-smoker.
  • You run 3 times a week and eat a healthy, balanced diet.
  • No particular stress at the moment. You feel well supported by friends and family.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are "not sure" what is causing it. Ask: "Am I going to die?" If asked what worries you, you are scared it is a heart attack. You want the doctor to "just fix me up".

The nurse and how Sarah changes

  • When asked, the nurse gives the triage observations (10:05; palpitations began about 09:35): HR 150 and regular on the monitor, BP 118/74, RR 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 °C, alert.
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, the nurse says: "I did one on arrival at 10:07. The examiner will give it to you in Part 2." Bloods were sent at 10:15 if the candidate asks.
  • If the candidate orders IV access, defibrillator pads, vagal manoeuvres or a medicine, the nurse says: "Will do, I'll set that up." The examiner notes it for credit in Part 2. Sarah stays in the same fast, regular rhythm throughout Part 1.
  • About 6 minutes into Part 1 (or when the examination starts if that is sooner), the nurse says: "Doctor, she's still 150 and regular on the monitor, and her BP is 114 over 72." Sarah says: "I feel a bit more woozy."
  • If the candidate lies Sarah back or explains calmly what is happening, she feels a little less woozy and a little calmer.

Exam findings

  • General: anxious young woman, alert, talking in full sentences, mildly increased work of breathing. Not pale, not sweaty.
  • Pulse: 150/min, regular, normal volume.
  • Blood pressure: 118/74 (114/72 after the nurse's report).
  • Perfusion: warm hands and feet, CRT under 2 seconds. GCS 15.
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Heart: rapid, dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Lungs: clear, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Legs: no ankle oedema, calves soft.
  • Hands: warm palms, fine tremor of the outstretched hands. No palmar erythema, no clubbing.
  • Neck: small, diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre that moves on swallowing. No nodules, no bruit, no lymphadenopathy.
  • Eyes: no exophthalmos, no lid retraction, no lid lag.
  • Reflexes (if tested): brisk but symmetrical.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as the intern, confirms Sarah's identity and gains consent.
Stays calm and reassuring while she is frightened. Uses plain language, acknowledges her fear of dying, and keeps the questions focused because she is still in the arrhythmia.
History
Characterises the palpitations:

kids.x: Onset: sudden, about 30 minutes ago, at rest
First episode, continuous since onset, has not stopped
Asks specifically whether the rhythm is regular or irregular, or asks her to tap it out (fast and regular)
Aggravating and relieving factors (none; relaxation did not help) and the impact (time off work)

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms and adverse features: chest pain, syncope or presyncope, breathlessness and ankle swelling. Elicits mild breathlessness and feeling faint, with no chest pain or syncope.
Asks cluster questions for causes in other systems:
check.d: Source scheme: three systems earns full marks, two systems earns partial. The hyperthyroidism cluster (7.1) must be one of them for the critical mark.

kids.x: Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, heat intolerance, loose bowel motions, anxiety, menstrual change (elicits the first four)
Phaeochromocytoma: previous episodes, sweating attacks, headache
Anaemia: pallor, fatigue, bleeding or heavy periods
Systemic or infective: fever, night sweats, rigors, chills

check.x: Asks specifically about SVT triggers and risk factors: caffeine (3 cups a day), alcohol (4 to 5 standard drinks a day on weekends), stimulants or recreational drugs, and previous cardiac or thyroid disease (none).

Takes the past history, medications and allergies needed before treatment: no past history, no asthma (relevant to adenosine), oral contraceptive pill, no over-the-counter medicines or recreational drugs, no allergies, and whether she could be pregnant.
Takes a family history: mother has coeliac disease, father well; asks about sudden or premature death, arrhythmia or thyroid disease in the family.
Takes a social history: teacher, lives alone, non-smoker, runs 3 times a week, healthy diet, no current stress, well supported.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: not sure of the cause, worried she will die of a heart attack, wants to be fixed.
Examination
Does a general inspection (anxious, alert, mildly breathless, not pale), reviews the vital signs and the monitor rhythm, and keeps her on continuous cardiac monitoring.
Assesses haemodynamic stability: pulse rate, rhythm and volume (150, regular), BP, peripheral perfusion and CRT, and conscious state.
Looks for heart failure and structural heart disease: JVP, heart sounds and murmurs, lung bases and ankle oedema.
Examines for thyroid disease: tremor and warm palms, palpates the thyroid (finds a diffuse smooth goitre), and checks the eyes for exophthalmos, lid retraction and lid lag.

Responds to the nurse's report that she is still at 150 and feels more woozy: reassesses her (BP, perfusion, chest pain, conscious state), asks for IV access and defibrillator pads, and calls the senior ED doctor. Also credit lying her back or starting vagal manoeuvres with a rhythm strip running.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: HR 150 is in the red zone at both sets, calling for a rapid response (in the ED, the senior doctor to the bedside now). RR, SpO2, BP, temperature and consciousness are in the white zone, so she is tachycardic but haemodynamically stable.
Reads the ECG systematically:

kids.x: Confirms the patient details, time and calibration
Rate about 150/min, regular rhythm, normal axis, narrow QRS
No P waves before the QRS complexes, with a pseudo r' in V1 and pseudo S in the inferior leads (very short RP); normal ST segments and T waves

check.x: Identifies a regular narrow complex tachycardia without preceding P waves as a supraventricular tachycardia (probably AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia).
States that a regular rate of about 150 should raise atrial flutter with 2:1 block, and that no flutter waves are seen (adenosine may unmask them if present).
Interprets the other bloods: normal haemoglobin (no anaemia), normal potassium and magnesium, normal renal function, and a negative beta-hCG.

Interprets the thyroid tests: suppressed TSH (under 0.01) with raised free T4 (32) and free T3 (11.5) is primary hyperthyroidism; the diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with no nodules makes Graves' disease most likely (requests TSH receptor antibodies to confirm), a likely trigger for the SVT.

Justifies the differentials, each with a feature for or against: sinus tachycardia from thyrotoxicosis, atrial fibrillation, AV re-entrant tachycardia through an accessory pathway (WPW), and anxiety or panic as a diagnosis of exclusion.
check.d: Phaeochromocytoma or anaemia with a feature against is an accepted alternative.

check.x: Management
States she is stable (no hypotension, chest pain, syncope, heart failure or reduced consciousness), and that if any appear she needs urgent synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation.
Sets up safely: resus or monitored bed, continuous monitoring, defibrillator pads on, large-bore IV access in the antecubital fossa, and a rhythm strip or 12-lead recording during every intervention.
Starts with vagal manoeuvres, preferably the modified Valsalva manoeuvre (strain, then lie flat immediately with the legs raised); carotid sinus massage is an alternative.
check.d: Full technique: semi-recumbent, strain by blowing into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to move the plunger for 15 seconds, then lie flat immediately with the legs raised to 45° for 15 seconds. Exact syringe size and timings are not required for credit.

check.x: If vagal manoeuvres fail, gives adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with a fast saline flush, then 12 mg if needed. Warns her beforehand about brief chest tightness, flushing and a feeling of doom, and confirms she has no asthma.
Names IV verapamil as the alternative to adenosine (for example in asthma), avoiding it with hypotension, poor LV function, a beta blocker or a wide complex rhythm.
After reversion, repeats the 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm to look for pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave) and observes her on the monitor.

Treats the thyrotoxicosis: beta blocker (such as propranolol) for symptom control once in sinus rhythm, discussion with endocrinology about an antithyroid drug (carbimazole) with baseline FBC and LFTs, and checks for features of thyroid storm (fever, confusion, heart failure).
Orders further investigations: a transthoracic echocardiogram, and Holter or event monitoring if episodes recur.

Explains in plain words that this is not a heart attack but a fast, regular 'short circuit' rhythm that is very treatable, triggered by an overactive thyroid. Answers 'Am I going to die?' honestly and kindly, and checks her understanding.
Safety netting
Tells her in plain words to call 000 or come straight to ED if the racing does not stop after trying the Valsalva manoeuvre, or if it comes with chest pain, fainting or bad breathlessness.
Teaches her the modified Valsalva manoeuvre to use for future episodes and advises cutting down caffeine and alcohol.

Arranges follow-up: GP review within about a week, endocrinology referral for Graves' disease, and cardiology referral (EP study and ablation if episodes recur). If carbimazole is started: stop it and get an urgent blood count for fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers; return for fever, confusion or worsening palpitations (thyroid storm).

part2.lead: Here are Sarah's observations, the 12-lead ECG the nurse recorded on arrival, and her blood results.
part2.patient:
Ask this straight after the examiner reads question 4. The candidate answers you directly as part of question 4.

  • "Am I going to die? Is it a heart attack?"
  • If thyroid is mentioned: "What has my thyroid got to do with my heart?"

You settle if the candidate explains clearly without jargon. If they say "SVT" or "adenosine" without explaining, ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. Palpitations began about 09:35. Monitor at both sets: regular narrow complex rhythm at 150/min. Any treatment ordered in Part 1 had not yet been given at 10:20. Treatment of the SVT should not wait for blood results.
handover.model:
• Read: HR 150 and regular at 10:05 and 10:20, in the red zone at both sets (Between the Flags adult zones, which apply on the NSW Adult Emergency Department observation chart). RR 20, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 118/74 then 114/72, temperature 37.4 °C, alert, CRT under 2 seconds: all white zone. At 10:20 she feels more light-headed and the nurse is concerned.
  • Meaning: a sustained tachycardia that is not settling, but with a maintained BP, normal perfusion and normal conscious state she is haemodynamically stable, so DC cardioversion is not needed now.
  • Changes: a red zone value calls for a rapid response. In the ED this means the senior doctor to the bedside now, a resus or monitored bed, pads on, and IV access before vagal manoeuvres and adenosine. Treatment does not wait for the blood results.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: palpitations, onset about 09:35; cardiac monitor on; 12-lead ECG at 10:07
Monitor unchanged at 150 regular; feels light-headed; doctor informed

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Sarah, 24-year-old woman, recorded 10:07 in the ED (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, standard calibration). Palpitations since about 09:35.

  • Rate: about 150/min.
  • Rhythm: regular, with fixed R-R intervals.
  • Axis: normal, about +60°.
  • P waves: no P waves visible before the QRS complexes. Pseudo r' wave in V1 and pseudo S waves in II, III and aVF (retrograde P waves at the end of the QRS; RP interval under 70 ms). No flutter waves in II, III, aVF or V1.
  • PR interval: cannot be measured.
  • QRS: 84 ms, narrow, normal morphology. No delta wave visible.
  • QT: 260 ms.
  • QTc: 410 ms (Bazett; less reliable at this rate).
  • ST segments and T waves: no significant ST deviation. T waves normal.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.

Conclusion: regular narrow complex tachycardia at about 150/min with retrograde P waves at the end of the QRS (pseudo r' V1, pseudo S II, III, aVF), consistent with typical AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia. No flutter waves. No ischaemic change.
handover.model:
• Read: confirms the patient details, the time and the calibration. Regular narrow complex tachycardia at about 150/min with a normal axis. No P waves before the QRS complexes, with a pseudo r' in V1 and pseudo S in the inferior leads (very short RP). Narrow QRS, normal ST segments and T waves, no old ECG.
  • Meaning: a regular narrow complex tachycardia with retrograde P waves at the end of the QRS and a very short RP interval is a supraventricular tachycardia, most likely AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (orthodromic AVRT usually has a longer RP, over 70 ms). A rate of 150 should always make you consider atrial flutter with 2:1 block. No flutter waves are seen here, and adenosine would unmask them if they were present. Sinus tachycardia would have a P wave before every QRS. AF would be irregular.
  • Changes: treat as stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine, with a rhythm strip running. Repeat the 12-lead in sinus rhythm to look for pre-excitation.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 10:15. Urgent results phoned through by the laboratory: FBC, electrolytes, magnesium, beta-hCG, TSH, free T4, free T3.
handover.model:
• Read: FBC normal (Hb 134). Sodium, potassium 4.0, creatinine and magnesium 0.85 normal. Serum beta-hCG negative. TSH is suppressed (under 0.01 mIU/L), and free T4 (32 pmol/L) and free T3 (11.5 pmol/L) are raised.
  • Meaning: suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and free T3 is primary hyperthyroidism. With the diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre and no nodules, Graves' disease is most likely; TSH receptor antibodies should be requested to confirm. This fits the weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools, anxiety and tremor. Thyrotoxicosis is the likely trigger for the SVT. No anaemia, and no electrolyte disturbance to correct. She is not pregnant.
  • Changes: send TSH receptor antibodies. Beta blocker for symptoms once in sinus rhythm. Discuss carbimazole with endocrinology, with baseline FBC and LFTs. Her contraception matters because antithyroid drugs carry pregnancy risks.

ask: You are now calling the emergency registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sarah, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sarah now, here in the emergency department.
Sarah has a question for you. Please answer her, then tell me what you would tell her before she goes home and what follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Sarah, 24, in the acute area.
  • Situation: sustained regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150 since about 09:35 (about 45 minutes); HR red zone, BP 114/72, SpO2 98% RA, alert, well perfused.
  • Background: sudden onset at rest, first episode; mild breathlessness and light-headedness, no chest pain or syncope. 4 months of weight loss, heat intolerance and loose stools; tremor and diffuse goitre. No asthma, on the OCP, no allergies.
  • Assessment: ECG: regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150, no P waves before the QRS, pseudo r' in V1 and pseudo S in the inferior leads (very short RP), no flutter waves: SVT, probably AVNRT. Suppressed TSH (under 0.01) with raised free T4 (32) and free T3 (11.5): primary hyperthyroidism, likely Graves' disease given the diffuse goitre (TRAb to confirm). FBC, electrolytes normal, beta-hCG negative. Stable SVT.
  • Recommendation: please review now; plan modified Valsalva then adenosine.

Supraventricular tachycardia, probably AVNRT, triggered by untreated thyrotoxicosis, most likely Graves' disease: sudden onset, regular rhythm at 150, narrow QRS with pseudo r' in V1 and pseudo S inferiorly (very short RP); weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools, tremor; suppressed TSH, raised free T4 and T3, diffuse goitre.

  • Atrial flutter with 2:1 block: for: rate 150. Against: no flutter waves.
  • Sinus tachycardia from thyrotoxicosis: for: thyrotoxic. Against: abrupt onset, fixed rate, no P before the QRS.
  • Atrial fibrillation: for: thyrotoxicosis. Against: regular rhythm.
  • AVRT (WPW): for: young, first episode. Against: the very short RP (pseudo r' in V1, under 70 ms) favours AVNRT; orthodromic AVRT usually has an RP over 70 ms. Pre-excitation can only be judged on a sinus-rhythm ECG.
  • Anxiety or panic: against: the ECG shows an arrhythmia.

1. Senior to bedside; monitored bed, pads on, large-bore antecubital IV, rhythm strip running.
  2. Stable (no hypotension, chest pain, syncope, heart failure or reduced consciousness). If unstable: synchronised DC cardioversion.
  3. Modified Valsalva: semi-recumbent, blow into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to move the plunger for 15 seconds, then lie flat immediately with legs raised to 45° for 15 seconds. Carotid sinus massage is an alternative.
  4. Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with saline flush, then 12 mg; warn her about transient chest tightness and doom; no asthma.
  5. Alternative: IV verapamil (not with hypotension, beta blocker or poor LV).
  6. Repeat 12-lead in sinus rhythm (delta wave?); observe.
  7. Thyrotoxicosis: send TRAb; propranolol for symptoms; discuss carbimazole with endocrinology, with baseline FBC and LFTs; check for thyroid storm.
  8. Echo; Holter if recurrent.

• Plain words: not a heart attack; a fast, regular "short circuit" rhythm, very treatable and rarely dangerous in a healthy heart, set off by an overactive thyroid.
  • Call 000 or come to ED if the racing does not stop after Valsalva, or comes with chest pain, fainting or bad breathlessness.
  • Teach the modified Valsalva; cut down caffeine and alcohol.
  • If carbimazole is started: stop it and get an urgent blood count for fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers; return for fever, confusion or worsening palpitations (thyroid storm).
  • Follow-up: GP within about a week; endocrinology referral for Graves' disease; cardiology referral (EP study and ablation if episodes recur).

ddx.dx: Supraventricular tachycardia (probable AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia) triggered by Graves' thyrotoxicosis
ddx.for: Sudden onset at rest of a fast regular rhythm she can tap out, a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150 with pseudo r' in V1 and pseudo S in the inferior leads (very short RP), and weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools, tremor, a diffuse smooth goitre, suppressed TSH and raised free T4 and T3.
ddx.against: A rate of exactly 150 also fits atrial flutter with 2:1 block, and thyrotoxicosis more often causes sinus tachycardia or AF.

ddx.for: The rate is regular at about 150 and she is thyrotoxic.
ddx.against: No flutter waves in II, III, aVF or V1, retrograde P waves at the end of the QRS (pseudo r' and pseudo S), and she is 24 with a structurally normal heart on examination.

ddx.for: She has clinical and biochemical hyperthyroidism with anxiety and tremor.
ddx.against: Onset was abrupt, the rate is fixed at 150, and there is no P wave before each QRS.

ddx.for: Thyrotoxicosis is a classic cause of AF.
ddx.against: She taps out a regular rhythm, the pulse is regular and the ECG has fixed R-R intervals.

ddx.dx: AV re-entrant tachycardia through an accessory pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White)
ddx.for: A young person with a first episode of regular narrow complex tachycardia.
ddx.against: The RP interval is very short (pseudo r' in V1, under 70 ms), which favours AVNRT; orthodromic AVRT usually has a longer RP (over 70 ms). Pre-excitation can only be judged on a sinus-rhythm ECG.

ddx.for: She feels anxious and on edge and slow breathing was tried first.
ddx.against: The ECG shows a sustained arrhythmia, and her anxiety is better explained by thyrotoxicosis; it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

guide:
In Part 1, Sarah answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. The nurse gives the triage observations when asked. If the candidate asks for the ECG or bloods, say they will be given in Part 2. About 6 minutes in, or as the examination begins, the nurse reports that Sarah is still at 150 and feels more woozy. Mark the bedside response (item 18) in Part 1. Treatment ordered in Part 1 (pads, IV access, vagal manoeuvres, adenosine, calling a senior) is noted and credited against the Management items in Part 2. Sarah stays in the same rhythm whatever is ordered in Part 1.

The history marks follow the source's scheme. Item 7 rewards cluster questions across systems (full credit for three systems). Item 5.3 needs a specific question about regularity or a request to tap out the rhythm, not just "describe it".

In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Sarah's question comes straight after question 4 is read. Credit a systematic ECG read whether it comes before or within the ISBAR. Accept carotid sinus massage as a vagal manoeuvre. Accept adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg (a further dose per local protocol is not penalised). Do not require verapamil or beta blocker doses.

A high-performing candidate establishes sudden onset, the regular rhythm and the absence of adverse features early. They screen the thyroid, phaeochromocytoma, anaemia and systemic clusters, ask about caffeine, alcohol and drugs, check for asthma before adenosine, and examine perfusion and the thyroid. In Part 2 they read the ECG as a regular narrow complex tachycardia with retrograde P waves, consider flutter at 150, and link the SVT to Graves' disease. They manage it as stable SVT with modified Valsalva, then adenosine with a warning, repeat the ECG in sinus rhythm, and plan the thyroid treatment and follow-up.

A borderline candidate does not ask whether the rhythm is regular, asks only cardiac questions and misses the thyroid symptoms, calls the ECG "sinus tachycardia" or "AF", jumps to DC cardioversion in a stable patient, gives adenosine without warning her, or does not connect the abnormal thyroid tests to the arrhythmia.
explain:
Diagnosis: SVT triggered by Graves' thyrotoxicosis

Sarah has a sudden-onset, sustained, regular tachycardia at about 150/min with a narrow QRS and no P waves before the QRS. There is a pseudo r' wave in V1 and pseudo S waves in II, III and aVF: retrograde P waves at the end of the QRS, with a very short RP interval. That is a supraventricular tachycardia, most likely AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), the commonest regular SVT in young women. She also has 4 months of weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools and anxiety, with a fine tremor and a diffuse goitre. A suppressed TSH (under 0.01) with a raised free T4 (32) and free T3 (11.5) confirms primary hyperthyroidism. The diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre without nodules makes Graves' disease most likely, and TRAb should be sent to confirm Graves' disease. Thyroid hormone increases sensitivity to adrenaline and noradrenaline, shortens atrial refractoriness and increases atrial ectopy, so it is a likely trigger. Thyrotoxicosis is a reversible trigger that should be treated because it makes episodes more likely, but the re-entry circuit itself persists, so recurrences are still possible once she is euthyroid; catheter ablation is the definitive treatment if they recur.

The history

On history alone it is hard to tell the arrhythmias apart, so ask specifically about regularity or ask the patient to tap the rhythm out. Sudden onset and offset with a fast, regular beat suggests a re-entrant SVT. An irregularly irregular beat suggests AF. Screen for adverse features (chest pain, syncope, breathlessness, heart failure). Then ask cluster questions for causes in other systems:

  • Endocrine: hyperthyroidism (weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools, anxiety, menstrual change); phaeochromocytoma (episodic palpitations, sweating, headache).
  • Haematological: anaemia (pallor, fatigue, bleeding).
  • Systemic: fever, night sweats, rigors, weight loss.

SVT triggers and risk factors are caffeine, alcohol, stimulants and recreational drugs, and previous cardiac or thyroid disease. Before treatment, ask about asthma (adenosine can cause bronchospasm), current medicines (beta blockers interact with verapamil) and pregnancy.

The examination

First decide whether the patient is stable: BP, perfusion, conscious state, chest pain and signs of heart failure. Then look for structural heart disease and the cause: tremor, warm palms, goitre and eye signs.

Interpreting the ECG

Work through it systematically: patient details and calibration, rate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR, QRS, ST segments, T waves, QTc and comparison. A regular narrow complex tachycardia has four main causes:

  • Sinus tachycardia: a P wave before every QRS, with gradual onset and offset.
  • AVNRT: P waves hidden in the QRS or just after it (pseudo r' or pseudo S waves).
  • AVRT (through an accessory pathway): retrograde P waves clearly separate from the QRS (RP over 70 ms), often in the ST segment.
  • Atrial flutter with 2:1 block: a rate of about 150, with sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF and V1.

When the rate is 150, always think of flutter. Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node, which terminates AVNRT and AVRT and unmasks flutter waves, so record a rhythm strip while giving it. A delta wave cannot be judged during the tachycardia, so repeat the 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm.

Acute management (eTG; ANZCOR Guideline 11.9)

  • Unstable (hypotension, chest pain, syncope, heart failure, reduced consciousness): urgent synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation.
  • Stable: continuous monitoring, defibrillator pads, a large-bore IV in the antecubital fossa and a running rhythm strip.
  • Vagal manoeuvres first. The modified Valsalva manoeuvre (semi-recumbent, strain for 15 seconds by blowing into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to move the plunger, then lie flat immediately with the legs raised to 45° for 15 seconds) works much more often than the standard Valsalva. Carotid sinus massage is an alternative in a young patient without a carotid bruit.
  • Adenosine 6 mg by rapid IV push followed immediately by a fast saline flush, then 12 mg if needed. Warn the patient beforehand about brief chest tightness, flushing, breathlessness and a sense of doom. This matters especially for a patient who is already afraid she is dying. Avoid in asthma or severe COPD (it can cause bronchospasm); use IV verapamil instead.
  • Verapamil IV is the alternative, for example in asthma. Avoid it with hypotension, poor LV function, beta blocker use or a wide complex or pre-excited rhythm.
  • After reversion: repeat the 12-lead ECG, observe, and discharge if well, with follow-up.

Treating the thyrotoxicosis

A beta blocker such as propranolol controls the adrenergic symptoms and reduces recurrence while the thyroid is treated. An antithyroid drug (carbimazole) is usually started with endocrinology advice, after baseline FBC and LFTs. Patients must be warned that fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers can mean agranulocytosis and need an urgent blood count. Carbimazole has pregnancy risks, so contraception and pregnancy plans are discussed (she is on the OCP and her beta-hCG is negative). Look for thyroid storm (fever, delirium, heart failure), which needs ICU-level care.

Further investigations and follow-up

Further investigations are a transthoracic echocardiogram for structural heart disease and LV function, and Holter or event monitoring for recurrent symptoms. She also needs repeat thyroid function tests on treatment. Refer her to cardiology, because an electrophysiology study and catheter ablation are curative for recurrent AVNRT or AVRT. Refer her to endocrinology for Graves' disease.

Safety netting

Teach her the modified Valsalva manoeuvre for future episodes. She should call 000 or come to ED if an episode does not stop, or comes with chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness. Advise her to cut down caffeine and alcohol. Arrange GP review within about a week.
points: Ask specifically whether palpitations are regular or irregular, or ask the patient to tap them out. Sudden onset of a fast, regular beat suggests a re-entrant SVT.
Always look for a cause in other systems: hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, anaemia and systemic illness, and ask about caffeine, alcohol and drugs.
A regular narrow complex tachycardia with no P waves before the QRS and retrograde P waves after it is an SVT. At a rate of 150, consider atrial flutter with 2:1 block.

Unstable SVT needs synchronised DC cardioversion. In stable SVT, use the modified Valsalva first, then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with a flush, then 12 mg, with a rhythm strip running and a warning to the patient beforehand.
After reversion, repeat the 12-lead ECG to look for pre-excitation (WPW), and arrange an echo and cardiology follow-up.

A suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and T3 and a diffuse, smooth goitre makes Graves' disease most likely; send TSH receptor antibodies to confirm. Control symptoms with a beta blocker, start an antithyroid drug with endocrinology, and warn about agranulocytosis (fever, sore throat).
